‘Lorca in New York: A Celebration’(through July 20) April is National Poetry Month, and among the celebrations is a three-month series of readings, screenings and other events focusing on the life and works of Federico García Lorca, the Spanish poet who at 38 was executed by pro-Franco forces at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War. Organized by the Federico García Lorca Foundation and Accion Cultural Española, the festivities coincide with Farrar, Straus & Giroux’s publication of a new edition of “Poet in New York,” a collection of poems that García Lorca wrote during his stay in New York City, from 1929 to 1930.
His time in the city — which included studying at Columbia — is the subject of “Back Tomorrow: Federico García Lorca/Poet in New York,” an exhibition of manuscripts, photographs and personal items on view through July 20 at the New York Public Library, Fifth Avenue and 42nd Street. A photograph, above right, of the poet with friends — he is at the far right — and his ink drawing “Self-Portrait With Flag and Fabulous Beast,” top, both from around 1929, are among the items that can be viewed Mondays and Thursdays through Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; Tuesdays and Wednesdays from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.; and Sundays from 1 to 5 p.m.; nypl.org; free.
His days at Columbia are the subject of a free lecture at the university on Monday at 6 p.m., given by Gonzalo Sobejano, a professor emeritus in the department of Latin American and Iberian cultures, at Butler Library, 515 West 114th Street, Morningside Heights. On Sunday at 7 p.m. the music that Lorca loved — flamenco and tango included — will be featured with his writing in a multimedia event at the Bowery Poetry Club, 308 Bowery, near Bleecker Street, East Village; $10. A schedule of events can be found at lorcanyc.com. (Anne Mancuso)
American Museum of Natural History: ‘Whales: Giants of the Deep’(daily) This interactive exhibition covering the world of the giant mammals, in context to humans and other animals, is on display through Jan. 5. Daily, from 10 a.m. to 5:45 p.m., Central Park West and 79th Street, (212) 769-5200,amnh.org. Timed tickets are necessary for the exhibition, with the suggested admission price of $25; $19 for students and 60+; $14.50 for children 12 and under.
Center for Jewish History: ‘Passages Through the Fire: Jews and the Civil War’(through Aug. 11) This exhibition sponsored by the American Jewish Historical Society and Yeshiva University Museum tells the stories of American Jews of the 1800s who were caught in the turmoil of the Civil War. It consists of more than 200 photographs, documents and other items from private collections, libraries and museums. Friday from 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.; Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; Monday, 5 to 8 p.m.; Wednesday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Admission, $8; $6 for students and 65+; free for under 5 and members and for everyone on Mondays, Wednesdays, 5 to 8 p.m. and all day Fridays. 15 West 16th Street, Flatiron district, (212) 294-8330,cjh.org.
Grady Alexis Gallery at El Taller Latino Americano: ‘Women Inspired’(through April 30) This group exhibition — including film; digital and alternative processes; photo collage; and mixed media — celebrates Women’s History Month. It features the work of 21 photographers who belong to the Professional Women Photographers group, an international nonprofit in New York City. Mondays through Thursdays, 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.; Fridays, 10:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.; Saturdays, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., Grady Alexis Gallery at El Taller, 2710 Broadway, third floor, at 104th Street, (212) 665-9460,tallerlatino.org; free.
Museum of Jewish Heritage: ‘Through Soviet Jewish Eyes: Photography, War, and the Holocaust’(Friday and Sunday) This is the last weekend for this exhibition of more than 50 rare images, which chronicled the daily hardships that Soviet Jews endured duringWorld War II, and is based on David Shneer’s book of the same title. Mr. Shneer is also the co-curator, with Lisa Tamiris Becker, of this exhibition. 36 Battery Place, Lower Manhattan, (646) 437-4202,mjhnyc.org; $12, $10 for 65+, $7 for students; free for members and children 12 and younger. Friday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5:45 p.m.
Museum of the Moving Image: ‘Spectacle: The Music Video’(through June 16) The history of the music video, from Vitaphone shorts of the 1920s to contemporary videos featuring Lady Gaga, is told in this exhibition of installations, projections and objects. Friday, 10:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Saturday and Sunday, 11:30 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Wednesday and Thursday, 10:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. 35th Avenue at 37th Street, Astoria, Queens, (718) 784-0077,movingimage.us; $12, $9 for students and 65+, $6 for children 3 to 12; free for members and children under 3.
New York Public LIbrary: ‘100 Years of Flamenco in New York’(through Aug. 3) This exhibition traces the popularity of the dance form in the city, from the mid-1800s to the present, through engravings and photographs, printed materials, costume pieces and films and recordings. Fridays, Saturdays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays from noon to 6 p.m.; Mondays and Thursdays from noon to 8 p.m.; New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, 111 Amsterdam Avenue, at 65th Street, Lincoln Center, (917) 275-6975,nypl.org/lpa; free.
New York Transit Museum: ‘Meet Miss Subways’ and ‘ElectriCity: Powering New York’s Rails’(continuing) Two exhibitions are on display. “Meet Miss Subways,” which looks at the beauty contest and the lives of former Miss Subways, up through June 2; and “ElectriCity: Powering New York’s Rails,” a historical display of items from the museum collection, including switches and circuit breakers, that illustrates how electricity powers the subway system. Tuesdays through Fridays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Boerum Place and Schermerhorn Street, Brooklyn Heights, (718) 694-1600,mta.info/mta/museum; $7, $5 for those ages 2 to 17 and 62+, free for members and for 62+ on Wednesdays.
‘On Time/Grand Central at 100’(through July 7) Events celebrating the terminal’s 100th anniversary keep growing. This multimedia exhibition, commissioned for the occasion, features 18 artists’ impressions of time, travel and the commuters who flood the terminal each day in pieces incorporating painting, video photography and sculpture. It can be viewed weekdays from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. New York Transit Museum Gallery Annex and Store, Grand Central Terminal, near the Station Masters’ Office, (212) 878-0106,grandcentralterminal.com/centennial; free.
The Skyscraper Museum: ‘The Woolworth Building @ 100’(through July 14) An exhibition celebrating the 100th anniversary of this Cass Gilbert-designed building — when completed in 1913 it was considered the tallest building in the world — features blueprints, photographs, contracts and other items. Wednesdays through Sundays from noon to 6 p.m., 39 Battery Place, Lower Manhattan, (212) 968-1961,skyscraper.org; $5, $2.50 for students and 65+.
New York Botanical Garden: The Orchid Show(Saturday through April 22) Thousands of orchids from all over the world are on display at this annual exhibition, returning for its 11th year. In addition to viewing the beauties during regular garden hours through April 22, guests can also take part in orchid care demonstrations, weekend concerts, and Q. and A. sessions. The “Orchid Evening” for this Saturday is sold out. A full schedule of events is atnybg.org. Bronx River Parkway (Exit 7W) and Fordham Road, the Bronx, (718) 817-8777; $25, $22 for students and 65+, $10 for children 2-12, free for children under 2. Discounts available for members. The garden is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Brooklyn Navy Yard Center at BLDG 92: ‘Reflections on Rosie’(Friday through Sunday, Wednesday and Thursday) The exhibition, “Reflections on Rosie,” contains the stories of women who worked at the Brooklyn Navy Yard during World War II and the female artists who now work in studios in the Center. The display, also sponsored by the Brooklyn Historical Society, includes oral histories and multimedia presentations and will be on view through May. Open Wednesdays through Sundays from noon to 6 p.m. Brooklyn Navy Yard Center at BLDG 92, 63 Flushing Avenue, at Carlton Avenue, (718) 907-5992,bldg92.org; free admission to exhibition.
Chelsea Community Center Street Fair(Saturday) From 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., on Avenue of the Americas, between 23rd and 32nd Streets.
‘Defiance’ Screening and Discussion(Monday) The story of the Bielski brothers, whose bravery and resourcefulness during the Nazi occupation of Belarus helped to save the lives of hundreds of Jews, was the basis of Nechama Tec’s 1993 book, “Defiance: The Bielski Partisans,” and Edward Zwick’s 2008 movie, starring Daniel Craig and Liev Schreiber. A screening of “Defiance,” at 7:30 p.m., will feature two special speakers: Zvi Bielski, son of Zus Bielski, one of the brothers, and Sally Frishberg, a Polish Holocaust survivor. The screening is a fund-raiser for School News Nationwide, a New York organization that promotes educational skills and tolerance. Symphony Space, 2537 Broadway, at 95th Street, (212) 864-5400,symphonyspace.org; $25.
Greek Independence Day Parade(Sunday) Sponsored by the Federation of Hellenic Societies of Greater New York, the parade begins at 1:30 p.m. at Fifth Avenue and 64th Street and continues north to 79th Street.
Museum of Jewish Heritage: Holocaust Remembrance Day(Monday and Wednesday) This solemn day of remembrance, beginning at sundown on Sunday, coincides this year with the 70th anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which inspired other resistance efforts. On Monday, a daylong Holocaust remembrance will feature stories from survivors from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.; visitors can also spend time in the museum’s galleries and memorial space. Free, but donations will be accepted. On Wednesday at 7 p.m., a performance of songs of resistance and mourning and other pieces from the time period presented by the Primo Levi Center will feature the Israeli singer Charlette Shulamit Ottolenghi; the Israeli pianist Shai Bachar; and Frank London, a trumpeter and member of the Klezmatics. Tickets are $15, $12 for students and 65+, $10 for members. 36 Battery Place, Lower Manhattan; (646) 437-4202;mjhnyc.org.
New York African Film Festival(Friday through Tuesday) This festival of works by veteran and emerging filmmakers will feature appearances by some of the directors and others involved with the movies. On Sunday, Haiti will be the focus of screenings and discussions, beginning at 1 p.m. with “Stones in the Sun,” a 2012 film by Patricia Benoit about Haitian immigrants in New York City. (It will also be shown on Friday at 1:30 p.m.) Ms. Benoit will introduce the film and take part in a discussion about it. At 3:30 p.m., “Toussaint Louverture,” a 2011 film by Philippe Niang, will be introduced by Jimmy Jean-Louis, who stars as the leader of the Haitian Revolution. He will also talk about the film after the screening, which commemorates the 210th anniversary of Louverture’s death. Screenings are at the Walter Reade Theater, 165 West 65th Street, and the Elinor Bunin Munroe Film Center, 144 West 65th Street; (212) 875-5601 or (212) 875-5600;africanfilmny.orgorfilmlinc.com; $13, $9 for students, $8 for members.
New York International Auto Show(Friday through Sunday) The show continues on Friday and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Daily tickets are $15 ($5 for those 12 and younger). Jacob K. Javits Convention Center, 655 West 34th Street, Manhattan, (212) 216-2000,autoshowny.com.
Pillow Fight NYC 2013(Saturday) The props may be soft, but there are some firm rules for this annual smacking of pillow-against-body event, which is one of many to take place around the world. Participants are advised to use only soft, feather-free pillows to swing lightly at one another, avoiding those without pillows or with cameras and to remove eyeglasses or sunglasses before combat. Pillows not to be donated need to be removed from the site. And, pajamas are optional. Presented by the Urban Playground Movement. From 3 to 6 p.m., Washington Square Park, Fifth Avenue and Waverly Place, Greenwich Village;2013.pillowfightday.com.
Tartan Week Events(Saturday and Sunday) The wearing of the kilts will be part — but not all — of events taking place during this annual celebration of Scottish pride. New music, including rap and hip-hop, will be offered by several Scottish bands including the Caledonia Collective at Webster Hall on Saturday; and the View and Stanley Odd at the Knitting Factory on Saturday; and the Bowery Ballroom on Sunday. Tickets are $25; $12.50 for children under 10; free for children under 5. And the 10-kilometer Scotland Run in Central Park will set off on Saturday at 8 a.m. from the West Drive near 67th Street; for details,nyrr.org. The full Tartan Week schedule is attartanweek.com.
Union Square Community Coalition Street Fair(Sunday) From 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Broadway, between 17th and 23rd Streets.
Talks About Writing and Hollywood(Friday and Tuesday) On Friday the writers Renata Adler (“Speedboat,” “Pitch Dark”) and David Shields (“Really Hunger,” “How Literature Saved My Life”) will discuss their craft to commemorate the reissue of Ms. Adler’s two novels. Both events begin at 7 p.m., Strand Book Store, 828 Broadway, at 12th Street, (212) 473-1452,strandbooks.com; purchase of one of the books or a $15 Strand book card is required.
NYC Discovery Tours: ‘The World of “Mad Men”: NYC During the Early 1960s’(Saturday and Sunday) This tour of Midtown sites associated with the time period and script locations for the AMC drama “Mad Men” include the Pan Am Building (now the MetLife Building), the Summit Hotel (now the Doubletree Metropolitan Hotel) and the Four Seasons (still the Four Seasons). At 12:15 p.m., with the meeting place given with reservations: (212) 465-3331; $20.
‘Union Square: Crossroads of New York’(Saturday) A tour focusing on the area’s political history meets at 2 p.m. by the statue of Lincoln in Union Square Park, near the 16th Street transverse. Sponsored by the Union Square Partnership. (212) 517-1826,unionsquarenyc.org; free.
Eileen C. Dugan Memorial 5K(Saturday) This run in Brooklyn Bridge Park — the 15th in memory of Ms. Dugan, a New York State assemblywoman from Brooklyn who died in 1996 at age 51 — will begin and end at Pier 6, Atlantic Avenue and Furman Street, Brooklyn Heights; start time is 9 a.m.; sold out. Information is available at15thdugan.eventbrite.com.
New York Colon Cancer Challenge(Sunday) Three events in commemoration of Colorectal Cancer Awareness Month are planned in Central Park. Presented by the New York Road Runners. Advance race fees are $37, $23 for members, $15 for those 18 and younger and 62+. Race-day registration: $40, $25 and $20. (212) 860-4455;nyrr.org.
Shorewalkers: ‘Walk Off the Lamb’(Saturday) This annual 16-mile walk travels along the Harlem and East Rivers from Inwood to the South Street Seaport and includes a stop for lunch in Carl Schurz Park. (212) 330-7686,shorewalkers.org; $3 donation.ANNE MANCUSO
